think:
1. Core Clinical Tension: A 32-year-old male resident of a tropical region presents with high fever, rigors, confusion, circulatory collapse, marked anemia, and acute left upper quadrant abdominal tenderness with guarding in the absence of trauma. This acute clinical picture mimics severe bacterial sepsis with peritonitis, occult intra-abdominal abscess, or an acute surgical hemoperitoneum secondary to primary splenic trauma or hematologic malignancy.
2. Admission Breakpoint: The presentation concludes following triage stabilization, vital signs, physical examination, initial baseline laboratory tests (CBC showing Hb 8 g/dL, normal WBC, normal platelets, normal BMP/LFTs/urinalysis/CXR), and bedside abdominal ultrasonography demonstrating free pelvic fluid and perisplenic hematoma, immediately prior to the confirmatory peripheral blood parasite smear and contrast CT.
3. Differential Distinctions: Severe bacterial sepsis with septic shock was suspected due to fever to 39.8°C, hypotension, and localized peritonitis, prompting blood cultures and empiric sepsis antibiotics; however, bacterial cultures remained sterile and circulatory collapse was attributable to severe parasitemia combined with intra-abdominal hemorrhage. Traumatic or hematologic atraumatic splenic rupture (e.g., leukemia, lymphoma, or infectious mononucleosis) was considered given the hemoperitoneum, but there was no history of trauma, normal white blood cell counts, normal coagulation profiles, and absence of primary splenic lesions on contrast CT. High parasitemia with rapid splenic congestion and reticuloendothelial hyperplasia precipitated spontaneous rupture.
case_prompt: A 32-year-old male presents to the emergency department with a 7-day history of dull, aching left upper quadrant abdominal pain accompanied by intermittent fever, rigors, drenching night sweats, anorexia, and generalized malaise. He denies cough, dyspnea, chest pain, diarrhea, jaundice, pruritus, or epistaxis, and reports no antecedent abdominal trauma. He is a resident of a tropical endemic region with a past history of uncomplicated febrile illnesses treated with oral therapy. On physical examination, he appears confused and pale, but without cyanosis or scleral icterus. Vital signs reveal a body temperature of 39.8°C, pulse rate of 110 beats per minute in sinus rhythm, blood pressure of 90/55 mm Hg, and oxygen saturation of 91% while breathing ambient air. Chest examination shows clear breath sounds bilaterally. Abdominal examination demonstrates left upper quadrant tenderness with localized involuntary guarding without generalized rigidity. Laboratory evaluation reveals a hemoglobin level of 8.0 g/dL, white blood cell count of 5,000/μL, and platelet count of 170,000/μL. Coagulation parameters, serum electrolytes, renal function tests, and liver function panels are all within normal ranges. Urinalysis and plain chest radiography are normal. Bedside abdominal ultrasonography reveals a large free fluid collection in the pelvis measuring 9.6 x 7.9 cm and a perisplenic hematoma without focal splenic parenchymal lesions.

diagnostic_reasoning.candidate: Severe bacterial sepsis / septic shock with intra-abdominal peritonitis
diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: High fever, altered mental status, localized abdominal guarding, and hemodynamic collapse prompted blood culture collection and empiric broad-spectrum antibiotic administration for septic shock, but blood cultures were negative and systemic decompensation was driven by severe parasitic hemolysis and internal hemorrhage.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: Blood cultures were taken, and an empirical dose of broad-spectrum antibiotics was administered as per local sepsis guidelines.

diagnostic_reasoning.candidate: Traumatic or hematologic splenic rupture / hematologic malignancy
diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: Hemoperitoneum with perisplenic hematoma raised suspicion for occult traumatic rupture or atraumatic rupture secondary to hematologic malignancy, but the patient denied trauma, displayed normal coagulation and leukocyte counts, and CT showed no underlying lymphoproliferative neoplasm.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: Severe P. falciparum infection was presumed as the underlying cause of spontaneous rupture of the spleen, as there was no evidence of other documented etiologies (i.e., traumatic, haematological, or infectious) for the splenic rupture.

diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: Peripheral blood microscopy demonstrated numerous intraerythrocytic ring stages with a high parasitemia index exceeding 5%, confirming severe malaria complicated by circulatory shock and a contrast-enhanced CT-verified grade II spontaneous subcapsular splenic rupture.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: Peripheral blood smears for malaria demonstrated multiple ring stages of P. falciparum with a high parasitemia index (PI) (>5%). He was diagnosed with severe malarial infection evident by circulatory collapse as per WHO guidelines... A contrast-enhanced computed tomography (CT) scan of the abdomen and pelvis demonstrated a 3 cm subcapsular splenic haematoma with free peritoneal fluids indicating grade II splenic rupture

editor_comments: Spontaneous splenic rupture is a rare, life-threatening complication of severe Plasmodium falciparum infection resulting from acute splenic congestion, microvascular thrombosis, and rapid architectural tension on the capsule. Clinicians must maintain high index of suspicion in endemic settings when acute left upper quadrant pain and circulatory collapse accompany high fever, and conservative splenic salvage should be pursued in hemodynamically stabilizable patients.
